# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** Associate
**Date:** November 20, 2026
**Re:** Riboul Solar Installations, LLC / Treikev Community Power, Inc. – Issues review of MSA and related project documents

**Privileged & Confidential – Attorney Work Product**

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed all nine documents in the folder:

- Master Services Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (MSA)
- Term Sheet dated January 21, 2026
- Order Form No. 1 (OF1)
- Statement of Work – New Jersey Rooftop Portfolio (SOW)
- Module tariff side letter
- Service Level Schedule (SLS)
- Quality Agreement (QA)
- Kickoff meeting notes
- Certificate of insurance

All of these documents appear to have been signed in March 2026. Construction is under way, and the target date for mechanical completion of all 14 Systems is December 15, 2026. That means the O&M and SLS regime is starting to apply now.

Because the documents are signed, each fix below will need a negotiated amendment with Treikev. The order of priority reflects Riboul's exposure.

| # | Issue | Where | Risk to Riboul | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Uncapped Site Damage indemnity that includes decades of lost Production Revenue | MSA §§ 11.1(b), 12.1–12.3; SOW § 1.6 | Uncapped, unwaivable liability for up to the full Offtake term of a System | **Highest** |
| 2 | Exclusivity is nationwide, covers all segments and has a 24-month tail | MSA § 9.1 (vs. Term Sheet § 4) | Shuts Riboul out of its other business lines and markets | **High** |
| 3 | New Jersey law and Mercer County courts in the Order Form override the MSA's Delaware choice | OF1 § 7 (vs. MSA §§ 17.1–17.2) | Split governing law, parallel forums, litigation in Treikev's home venue | **High** |
| 4 | The SLS imports the QA's broad "Defect" definition | SLS § 1.2; QA § 1.3 | SLA deadlines and service credits apply to failures Riboul did not cause, including Treikev's modules | **Medium–High** (now live) |

**The common thread is the order of precedence.** Under **MSA § 2.3**, documents control in this order:

1. Order Form
2. Statement of Work
3. Service Level Schedule
4. Body of the MSA
5. Quality Agreement

So the Order Form, the SOW and the SLS each prevail over the body of the MSA. Three of the four issues arise because a project-level document overrides, or fills in, a protection Riboul negotiated in the MSA body.

---

## 2. Issues

### Issue 1 – Site Damage indemnity: uncapped liability for long-term lost revenue

**Where:**
- MSA § 11.1(b), the indemnity for "Site Damage, as such term is defined in the applicable Statement of Work"
- MSA § 12.3, the carve-out from §§ 12.1 and 12.2
- SOW § 1.6(b), the definition of Site Damage

**What the documents say:**
- **MSA § 11.1(b)** requires Riboul to indemnify Treikev for Losses arising from Site Damage "arising from the performance of the Services." The closing paragraph of § 11.1 extends this to Losses Treikev suffers directly, "whether or not a third-party claim is asserted." In effect this is a first-party damages claim, not just a third-party indemnity.
- **MSA § 12.3** provides that the § 12.2 cap (fees paid or payable in the prior 12 months) **and** the § 12.1 waiver of consequential damages, lost profits, lost revenue and lost production "shall not apply to Provider's obligations under Section 11.1(b)."
- **SOW § 1.6** defines Site Damage to include:
  - (a) physical damage to the roof and premises; and
  - (b) "any lost Production Revenue resulting from that damage … for the remaining term of the Offtake Agreement for the affected System."
- **SOW §§ 1.4–1.5** define Production Revenue broadly. It covers community solar subscription revenue, bill credits, PPA revenue and Environmental Attributes (SRECs/TRECs) that Treikev "receives or would have received."

**Why it matters for Riboul:**
- **No cap and no waiver.** The Site Damage indemnity is **not** subject to the 12-month fees cap, and lost revenue is **not** excluded. The § 12.1 waiver that would normally exclude lost revenue is switched off for exactly this obligation.
- **Ordinary events can trigger it.** Consider a roof leak at a penetration, membrane damage during installation, or damage that forces a System offline for investigation or repair. Any of these could let Treikev claim lost subscription and attribute revenue for the **entire remaining Offtake term**. New Jersey community solar subscriptions and offtake arrangements commonly run up to about 20 years. The SOW language even reaches revenue lost while a System is "curtailed to allow investigation."
- **The exposure is large.** The Portfolio is 18.6 MWdc across 14 roofs, with Systems up to 2.0 MWdc (NJ-07). A single damaged roof could support a claim many times the annual O&M fee (about $176,700 per year for the whole Portfolio). It could also exceed the Installation Fee for that System.
  - These figures are only illustrative. Actual exposure depends on offtake pricing and mitigation, which we have not seen.
- **Weak causation standard.** The trigger is only "arising from the performance of the Services." There is no negligence standard and no "to the extent caused by" comparative-fault language, unlike § 11.1(a).
- **Not consistent with the deal.** Term Sheet § 8.2 contemplated a *mutual* waiver of lost revenue and lost production. § 8.4 contemplated carve-outs "consistent with market practice." An uncapped carve-out for decades of a developer's project revenue is not market practice for an installer.
- **Insurance will not cover it.** The CGL policy ($2M per occurrence / $4M aggregate) and the $5M umbrella shown on the certificate of insurance are not designed to absorb long-tail economic loss of this kind. Much of the exposure would be uninsured.
- **Precedence does not help.** The SOW ranks above the MSA body under § 2.3. Riboul therefore cannot argue that MSA § 12.1's general lost-revenue exclusion overrides the SOW definition.
- **Overlap with the warranty.** The 10-year roof penetration warranty (MSA § 8.2) already obliges Riboul to repair leaks. The Site Damage indemnity layers uncapped revenue loss on top of that remedy.

**Recommended fix (in order of preference):**
1. **Delete SOW § 1.6(b)** so that Site Damage means physical damage to the roof and premises only.
2. **Amend MSA § 12.3** so that § 11.1(b) is carved out of the **cap only**, not the § 12.1 consequential and lost-revenue waiver. Better still, put Site Damage under a separate super-cap, for example the greater of a fixed dollar amount tied to available insurance and a multiple of the fees for the affected System.
3. If Treikev insists on some lost-revenue recovery, take a fallback position on lost Production Revenue:
   - limit it to the period reasonably required to repair, for example a maximum of 90–180 days;
   - cap it per System and in the aggregate;
   - require Treikev to mitigate; and
   - credit any insurance or business-interruption proceeds.
4. Add a fault standard: "to the extent caused by the negligence or breach of Provider or its subcontractors." Exclude pre-existing roof conditions, building owner or tenant acts, and Customer-Furnished Equipment. This would be consistent with MSA § 11.2(c).
5. Add a precedence override: no SOW or Order Form definition may expand Riboul's liability under Sections 11 or 12 unless it expressly states that it amends those Sections.

---

### Issue 2 – Exclusivity far broader than agreed

**Where:**
- MSA § 9.1
- MSA § 15.4, under which Section 9 survives termination
- Compare Term Sheet § 4

**What the documents say:**
- **MSA § 9.1** applies "during the Term and for a period of twenty-four (24) months following the expiration or termination" of the MSA. It bars Riboul, directly or through any Affiliate, from performing "solar photovoltaic installation, engineering, procurement and construction, or operations and maintenance services for any person other than Customer and its Affiliates **anywhere in the United States**."
- **Term Sheet §§ 4.1–4.3** set out the agreed exclusivity:
  - **Scope:** only commercial rooftop community solar projects in **New Jersey and Pennsylvania**.
  - **Duration:** **Initial Term only**, with "no post-term restriction."
  - **Carve-outs:** Riboul's residential, utility-scale, ground-mount and out-of-region business is expressly unrestricted.
- Nothing in the side letter, OF1, the SOW or the other documents narrows § 9.1.

**Why it matters for Riboul:**
- **It is a full non-compete.** Read literally, § 9.1 bars Riboul from any solar installation or O&M work for anyone other than Treikev nationwide. That includes residential, utility-scale, ground-mount and C&I work outside New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Riboul may already be in breach if it has other active customers. We should confirm this with the client immediately.
- **It runs much longer than agreed.** The Term is three years from March 2, 2026 and then auto-renews (MSA § 15.1). The restriction continues for 24 months after the Term ends, so it could last five years or more. Treikev, by contrast, gives only a non-binding right of first proposal (MSA § 9.2) and no volume commitment. It can also terminate any Order Form for convenience on 30 days' notice (MSA § 15.3).
- **Enforceability is uncertain, which cuts both ways.** Delaware and New Jersey courts generally review restrictive covenants for reasonableness of scope, geography and duration. A court might decline to enforce § 9.1, or might blue-pencil it. But Riboul should not rely on litigating enforceability:
  - the uncertainty itself chills Riboul's business;
  - it gives Treikev leverage in any dispute; and
  - under the § 18.5 severability clause, a court may enforce the clause "to the maximum extent permitted" rather than strike it.
- **Departure from the term sheet.** The term sheet is expressly non-binding (§ 12), so Riboul cannot simply enforce it. However, the MSA has no entire-agreement clause, and the term sheet is clear evidence of the agreed bargain. That is helpful negotiating leverage and could be relevant to interpretation.

**Recommended fix:**
- Replace § 9.1 with the Term Sheet § 4 formulation:
  - restriction limited to installation and O&M services for third parties on **commercial rooftop community solar projects in New Jersey and Pennsylvania**;
  - applies **during the Initial Term only**;
  - express carve-outs for residential, utility-scale, ground-mount and out-of-region work.
- Delete the 24-month post-term tail. Remove Section 9.1 from the survival list in § 15.4, keeping only § 9.3 (non-solicitation, which matches Term Sheet § 4.5).
- Consider making exclusivity fall away if Treikev terminates OF1 for convenience, or if Treikev offers Riboul no new work over a set period.
- Ask the client now about any existing third-party engagements so that we can assess current breach exposure and, if needed, obtain a waiver from Treikev.

---

### Issue 3 – The Order Form's New Jersey law and Mercer County forum override the MSA's Delaware choice

**Where:**
- OF1 §§ 7.1–7.2
- Compare MSA §§ 17.1–17.2 and § 2.3, and Term Sheet §§ 11.1–11.2

**What the documents say:**
- **MSA § 17.1:** Delaware law. **MSA § 17.2:** exclusive jurisdiction of the state or federal courts in Wilmington, Delaware. Term Sheet § 11 also contemplated Delaware law and a Wilmington forum.
- **OF1 § 7.1:** OF1, the Portfolio SOW "and all Services performed under them" are governed by "the laws of the State of New Jersey."
- **OF1 § 7.2:** exclusive jurisdiction of the **Superior Court of New Jersey, Mercer County**. Treikev's offices are in Princeton, Mercer County.
- **MSA § 2.3** ranks the Order Form first. Under **MSA § 2.2**, each Order Form and its SOW forms a separate contract.

**Why it matters for Riboul:**
- **The New Jersey choice controls the live project.** The Delaware provisions are effectively displaced for OF1, which is the entire current engagement: 18.6 MWdc and a $25,668,000 Installation Fee. That covers:
  - installation disputes;
  - payment disputes;
  - O&M disputes, because SLS obligations are Services performed under OF1 and the SOW; and
  - probably Site Damage claims.
- **Delaware still governs at the MSA level.** For example, exclusivity under § 9.1 would remain under Delaware law. This creates:
  - **split governing law**, with possibly different results on indemnity, limitation-of-liability and restrictive-covenant questions;
  - a risk of **parallel proceedings** in Wilmington and Mercer County over related claims; and
  - forum-fight costs at the start of any dispute.
- **Home-court advantage for Treikev.** Mercer County is Treikev's home venue. Three of the Sites (NJ-03, NJ-07, NJ-14) are also in Mercer County.
- **Loss of a negotiated term.** Riboul loses the neutral Delaware choice it negotiated and has to analyse questions such as indemnity enforceability, the scope of the consequential-damages waiver and the enforceability of the restrictive covenant under New Jersey law.
- **The jury waiver may not carry over cleanly.** MSA § 17.4 still applies by incorporation, but its effect in a New Jersey court applying New Jersey law should be confirmed.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend OF1 to **delete § 7**. Alternatively, replace it with: "This Order Form is governed by Sections 17.1 through 17.4 of the MSA."
- Amend **MSA § 2.3** to say that, notwithstanding the order of precedence, Sections 9, 11, 12 and 17 of the MSA control unless an Order Form expressly identifies the MSA Section it modifies and states that it overrides that Section. This prevents the same problem in future Order Forms.
- If Treikev insists on New Jersey law for the project, because of local regulatory and lien-law considerations, a possible fallback is:
  - accept New Jersey law for OF1 only;
  - require a single forum for all disputes under the MSA and all Order Forms (preferably federal court, or at least a neutral county);
  - confirm the jury waiver and escalation process; and
  - add a consolidation clause.

---

### Issue 4 – The Service Level Schedule imports an over-broad "Defect" definition

**Where:**
- SLS § 1.2, which cross-refers to QA § 1.3
- SLS § 3.2, the 5-Business-Day Remediation Period
- SLS § 4, service credits
- Compare MSA § 1.4

**What the documents say:**
- **MSA § 1.4:** "Defect" means "a failure of Provider's Installation Work to conform to the Specifications." This is a workmanship-based concept, consistent with the warranty exclusions in MSA § 8.4.
- **SLS § 1.2:** in the SLS, "Defect" "has the meaning given in Section 1.3 of the Quality Agreement."
- **QA § 1.3:** a Defect is any nonconformity, malfunction, damage, deterioration or performance shortfall in a System or any component, "**whether or not caused by Provider**." It expressly includes **Customer-Furnished Equipment**, such as the Halvorne modules Treikev supplies and the Customer-owned meters. In the QA this definition only drives logging and reporting under QA § 5.
- **SLS § 3.2:** Riboul must remediate **each Defect within 5 Business Days** after notice.
- **SLS § 4:** daily service credits for late remediation (5% or 2% of the Monthly O&M Fee per Business Day), plus response credits, up to 100% of the monthly fee per System.
- **SLS § 5.3:** chronic-failure root cause analysis, with the risk of termination for material breach under MSA § 15.2 preserved by SLS § 4.7.
- The SLS ranks **above** the MSA body under § 2.3, so the broad imported definition prevails over MSA § 1.4 for SLA purposes.

**Why it matters for Riboul:**
- **Riboul becomes responsible for things it did not cause.** It would have to fix, within 5 Business Days and under service credits:
  - module failures;
  - meter failures;
  - damage caused by building owners, tenants or third parties;
  - weather-related deterioration; and
  - any "shortfall against expected performance," whatever the cause.
- **Remediation may be out of Riboul's hands.** Module replacement depends on Treikev's spare modules (SOW § 9.3) and on manufacturer warranty processes that Treikev controls (MSA §§ 3.5, 8.3). The SLS § 3.5 extensions cover only force majeure and access failures, not Customer-Furnished Equipment.
- **Conflict with the agreed allocation.** The SLS conflicts with MSA § 3.5 and § 8.4 and with Term Sheet § 3.3, under which Treikev keeps responsibility for Customer-Furnished Equipment. It also undercuts SOW § 9.4, under which repairs of Customer-Furnished Equipment are paid out-of-scope work at Annex C rates.
- **Treikev could argue that out-of-scope repairs are covered by the O&M fee.** Its argument would be that the SLS obliges Riboul to remediate all Defects as part of the O&M Services.
- **The fee is small relative to the risk.** The O&M fee (about $14,725 per month for the Portfolio) does not price this risk. Credits can wipe out a System's monthly fee, and repeated "failures" could support a material breach and termination narrative.
- **Timing.** This becomes live as each System is accepted. Several should already be at or near acceptance.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend **SLS § 1.2** so that "Defect" means a failure of Provider's Installation Work, Provider-supplied equipment or O&M Services to conform to the Specifications or the SOW. In other words, track MSA § 1.4 and expressly exclude:
  - Customer-Furnished Equipment;
  - conditions caused by Customer, building owners, tenants or third parties;
  - unapproved modifications; and
  - force majeure.
- Add to SLS § 3.5 an extension or suspension of the Remediation Period and of credits where remediation depends on Customer-Furnished Equipment, spare modules, manufacturer warranty action or Customer approvals.
- State that Riboul's only obligations for excluded conditions are to log and report them (QA §§ 5.1, 5.3) and to perform any repair on request as out-of-scope work under SOW § 9.4 at Annex C rates.
- Add a sentence to QA § 1.3 stating that the definition applies only for inspection, logging and reporting and creates no remediation, warranty or service-credit obligation.

---

## 3. Other observations (lower priority)

- **Order of precedence generally (MSA § 2.3).** Any future Order Form or SOW could again override core MSA protections without notice. The amendment proposed under Issue 3 should be drafted to protect Sections 9, 11, 12 and 17 globally.
- **Liability cap base (MSA § 12.2).** During construction the 12-month fees figure is large, because it includes the Installation Fee. During a long O&M tail it shrinks to about the annual O&M fee. This is acceptable as drafted, but it shows why the Site Damage carve-out matters so much.
- **Side letter.** The tariff mechanism matches Term Sheet § 6.3. Modules stay at Treikev's risk (side letter § 2.1), and adjustments for Provider-supplied Covered Equipment are reasonable. One practical point: Riboul must give notice within 20 Business Days of becoming aware of a Tariff Change (side letter § 4.1), so the client should calendar this. No legal issue was identified.
- **Certificate of insurance and kickoff notes.** The certificate appears to meet MSA § 13.1:
  - CGL $2M / $4M with products-completed operations;
  - auto $1M;
  - employer's liability $1M;
  - umbrella $5M;
  - installation floater at full replacement value;
  - all insurers rated A- VII or better;
  - additional insureds endorsed.

  The kickoff notes are operational and state that they do not amend the contract documents (§ 2.3). Neither document raises an issue. As noted, though, the insurance program will not respond to the lost-revenue exposure in Issue 1.

---

## 4. Recommended next steps

1. **Client call.** Explain Issues 1 and 2 and confirm whether Riboul has any current or pipeline work that § 9.1 would catch.
2. **Prepare an Amendment No. 1** covering:
   - SOW § 1.6(b);
   - MSA §§ 9.1, 12.3, 15.4 and 2.3;
   - OF1 § 7; and
   - SLS §§ 1.2 and 3.5, plus the QA § 1.3 clarifying sentence.
3. **Negotiating position.** Rely on the term sheet (§§ 4, 8.2, 11) as the record of the agreed deal for Issues 1–3. For Issue 4, rely on Treikev's own allocation of responsibility for Customer-Furnished Equipment in MSA §§ 3.5 and 8.4 and Term Sheet § 3.3.
4. **Interim operational guidance.** Until the amendment is signed, Riboul should:
   - document carefully any roof condition issues found in pre-construction surveys and Hold Point photos, which will be key evidence against Site Damage claims;
   - in each Notice of Defect, record whether the issue relates to Customer-Furnished Equipment, and promptly dispute any service credits claimed for such issues under SLS § 4.6; and
   - reserve rights in writing on the "Defect" definition.

Happy to turn this into a client-facing advice letter and a markup of the amendment.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** Associate
**Date:** November 20, 2026
**Re:** Riboul Solar Installations, LLC / Treikev Community Power, Inc.: issues in the MSA document set affecting Riboul as Provider

---

## Executive Summary

I reviewed all nine documents in the folder:

- Master Services Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (MSA)
- Term Sheet dated January 21, 2026
- Order Form No. 1
- Statement of Work – New Jersey Rooftop Portfolio (SOW)
- Module tariff side letter
- Service Level Schedule
- Quality Agreement
- Kickoff meeting notes
- Certificate of insurance

Three issues need the client's attention. In order of priority:

1. **Uncapped, multi-decade lost revenue exposure through the Site Damage indemnity** (MSA §§ 11.1(b), 12.3; SOW § 1.6). This is the most serious financial risk.
2. **Overbroad exclusivity** (MSA § 9.1). The clause is nationwide, covers all solar segments, and runs for 24 months after the term. That is well beyond the agreed deal in Term Sheet § 4.
3. **Governing law and forum conflict** (Order Form No. 1 § 7). New Jersey law and Mercer County courts override the MSA's Delaware choice for the entire current project.

One background point affects all three issues. **MSA § 2.3 sets the order of precedence as follows: Order Form, then SOW, then Service Level Schedule, then the MSA body, then Quality Agreement.** The Order Form, the SOW and the Service Level Schedule therefore all prevail over the body of the MSA. This matters for Issues 1 and 3, because in each case a provision in a higher-ranking document either changes or controls the MSA.

---

## Issue 1: Uncapped Site Damage Indemnity Extending to Lost Production Revenue

**Where:** MSA § 11.1(b) and § 12.3, read with SOW § 1.6 (and SOW §§ 1.4–1.5).

**What the documents say.**

- **The indemnity.** MSA § 11.1(b) requires Riboul to indemnify Treikev for Losses arising from "Site Damage, as such term is defined in the applicable Statement of Work." The last paragraph of § 11.1 extends this to Losses Treikev suffers directly, "whether or not a third-party claim is asserted."
- **The carve-out.** MSA § 12.3 provides that the § 12.2 cap (fees paid or payable in the prior 12 months) and the § 12.1 exclusion of consequential damages, lost profits, lost revenue and lost production "shall not apply to Provider's obligations under Section 11.1(b)."
- **The definition.** SOW § 1.6 defines Site Damage in two parts:
  - (a) physical damage to the roof and premises; and
  - (b) "any lost Production Revenue resulting from that damage … for the remaining term of the Offtake Agreement for the affected System."
- **What "Production Revenue" covers.** It is defined broadly in SOW § 1.5 to include subscription bill credits and Environmental Attributes. Offtake Agreements under SOW § 1.4 include New Jersey Community Solar Energy Program subscriptions, which typically run for 15–20 years or more.

**Why it matters for Riboul.** None of these provisions is unusual on its own. Read together, however, they mean that any roof damage connected with Riboul's work could expose Riboul to Treikev's lost project revenue for the rest of the offtake term. That liability would have no cap and could not be excluded as consequential loss. The following points make this worse:

- **The trigger is low.** Lost revenue is recoverable for any period a System is "offline, de-energized or curtailed to allow investigation or repair." A roof leak investigation alone could start the clock.
- **It is a first-party claim.** No third party needs to sue. Treikev can claim directly.
- **The scale is large.** The Portfolio is 18.6 MWdc across 14 Sites, so the potential revenue stream is very large compared with the roughly $25.7 million Installation Fee and the roughly $176,700 annual O&M fee.
- **The precedence clause does not help.** The SOW ranks above the MSA body under § 2.3, so the broad definition controls. Nothing in the MSA body limits it.
- **It departs from the Term Sheet.** Term Sheet § 8.2 records a *mutual* waiver of lost revenue and lost production, and § 8.4 states that carve-outs would be "consistent with market practice." An uncapped carve-out covering decades of lost revenue is not market practice for an installation contractor.
- **Insurance will not cover it.** The certificate of insurance shows CGL ($2M/$4M) and umbrella ($5M) coverage. These policies respond to property damage, not to pure economic loss from lost offtake revenue. A contractual assumption of lost revenue would very likely be uninsured.

**Recommended fix (in order of preference):**

1. **Narrow the definition.** Amend SOW § 1.6 to delete limb (b), so that Site Damage means physical damage to the roof and premises only.
2. **Restore the waiver.** Amend MSA § 12.3 so that the § 12.1 consequential damages exclusion applies to § 11.1(b). Lost Production Revenue would then be excluded whatever the SOW says.
3. **If Treikev insists on some uncapped property damage coverage:**
   - keep the cap carve-out only for physical Site Damage, ideally limited to amounts covered by Riboul's insurance; and
   - put any lost revenue element under a separate sub-cap (for example, a fixed dollar amount or a limited number of months of revenue per System), with a short duration limit.
4. **Add a conflicts clause.** State expressly in the MSA that § 12 controls notwithstanding § 2.3, so that a later SOW cannot reintroduce this exposure.

---

## Issue 2: Exclusivity Overbroad and Inconsistent with the Term Sheet

**Where:** MSA § 9.1, compared with Term Sheet § 4.

**What the documents say.**

- **MSA § 9.1.** Riboul may not, directly or through any Affiliate, perform "solar photovoltaic installation, engineering, procurement and construction, or operations and maintenance services for any person other than Customer and its Affiliates anywhere in the United States." The restriction applies "during the Term and for a period of twenty-four (24) months following the expiration or termination of this Agreement."
- **Term Sheet § 4 records a much narrower deal:**
  - **Scope** (§ 4.1): commercial rooftop community solar projects in New Jersey and Pennsylvania only.
  - **Duration** (§ 4.2): the Initial Term only, with "no post-term restriction."
  - **Unrestricted business** (§ 4.3): Riboul's residential, utility-scale, ground-mount and out-of-region business is expressly not restricted.

  Nothing in the side letter, the Order Form or any other document narrows § 9.1.

**Why it matters for Riboul.**

- **It shuts down Riboul's other business.** Read literally, § 9.1 bars all of Riboul's non-Treikev work, including residential, utility-scale, ground-mount, commercial non-community-solar work and every project outside New Jersey and Pennsylvania. It also binds Riboul's Affiliates. This is effectively a sole-customer arrangement for Riboul's whole business.
- **There is a serious mismatch in consideration.** Treikev's reciprocal commitment in MSA § 9.2 is only a right of first proposal, with no obligation to award work. Treikev can also terminate any Order Form for convenience on 30 days' notice (§ 15.3). Riboul could therefore be barred from all other work while receiving none from Treikev.
- **The tail is long and starts at an uncertain point.** The Term includes automatic one-year Renewal Terms (§ 15.1), and § 9 survives termination (§ 15.4). The restriction could run for the 3-year Initial Term plus any renewals plus 2 years. Termination for cause by Treikev would also trigger the 24-month tail.
- **Enforceability is not a safe answer.** A Delaware court applying a reasonableness review might refuse to enforce the clause or blue-pencil it. Riboul should not rely on that, because:
  - Delaware courts have at times declined to blue-pencil overbroad restrictive covenants;
  - § 18.5 (severability) may invite a court to enforce the clause "to the maximum extent permitted"; and
  - for the active work, the governing law question in Issue 3 adds uncertainty about which state's restrictive covenant law applies.
- **The Term Sheet is not binding, but it is useful.** Term Sheet § 12 makes the exclusivity terms non-binding, so Riboul cannot enforce § 4 directly. It is, however, strong leverage in renegotiation, because the MSA clause departs clearly from the documented commercial deal.

**Recommended fix.** Replace MSA § 9.1 so that it tracks Term Sheet § 4:

- **Scope:** installation and O&M services for third parties on *commercial rooftop community solar projects in New Jersey and Pennsylvania*.
- **Duration:** the *Initial Term only*. Delete the 24-month post-term tail and make clear that the restriction does not run during Renewal Terms unless separately agreed.
- **Carve-out:** add an express statement, as in Term Sheet § 4.3, that residential, utility-scale, ground-mount and out-of-region work is unrestricted.
- **Early release:** consider a provision that ends exclusivity if Treikev terminates for convenience or materially breaches, or if Treikev fails to award a minimum volume of work under § 9.2.
- **Survival:** remove § 9.1 from the survival list in § 15.4. The § 9.3 non-solicitation can continue to survive for 12 months, which matches Term Sheet § 4.5.

---

## Issue 3: Order Form No. 1 Overrides the MSA's Delaware Governing Law and Forum

**Where:** Order Form No. 1 § 7, compared with MSA §§ 17.1–17.2 and § 2.3.

**What the documents say.**

- **The MSA.** MSA § 17.1 selects Delaware law, and § 17.2 gives exclusive jurisdiction to the state or federal courts in Wilmington, Delaware. Term Sheet § 11 records the same agreed position.
- **Order Form No. 1.** Section 7.1 provides that the Order Form, "the Portfolio SOW and all Services performed under them are governed by the laws of the State of New Jersey." Section 7.2 submits the parties to the exclusive jurisdiction of the Superior Court of New Jersey, Mercer County.
- **Precedence.** MSA § 2.3 puts the Order Form first. MSA § 2.2 also provides that each Order Form with its SOW "forms a separate contract."

**Why it matters for Riboul.**

- **New Jersey law and forum control the entire live project.** Because of the precedence clause, the New Jersey provisions govern disputes over the whole 18.6 MWdc Portfolio, which is all of Riboul's current work under the relationship. The Delaware choice would govern only the MSA in the abstract.
- **Riboul would litigate in Treikev's home venue.** Treikev's offices are in Princeton, Mercer County, and three of the Sites (NJ-03, NJ-07, NJ-14) are in Mercer County.
- **Riboul loses the Delaware position it negotiated.** Both parties are Delaware entities, and Delaware was agreed in the Term Sheet.
- **There is a real risk of split law and parallel proceedings.** A single dispute could involve both MSA terms (for example, indemnity, the liability cap or exclusivity) and Order Form or SOW terms (for example, fees, Site Damage or the SOW scope). The parties could then argue over which law and which exclusive forum applies, and could end up with proceedings in both Wilmington and Mercer County. Two "exclusive" forum clauses pointing in different directions invite satellite litigation.
- **Substantive consequences follow.** New Jersey law would govern the interpretation of the Site Damage definition in Issue 1 and possibly the enforceability analysis for the cap carve-outs. It may also bring in New Jersey contractor-specific rules. The jury waiver in MSA § 17.4 is drafted for "this Agreement," and its application in a New Jersey court proceeding on the Order Form should not be assumed.

**Recommended fix.**

1. **Amend Order Form No. 1** to delete § 7 entirely, by a short amendment signed by both parties under MSA § 18.4, so that MSA § 17 governs.
2. **Amend MSA § 2.3** to add that Sections 12 and 17 of the MSA control over any conflicting provision of an Order Form, SOW, Service Level Schedule or Quality Agreement unless that document expressly states that it amends the specified MSA section. This protects against the same problem in future Order Forms.
3. **Fallback if Treikev insists on New Jersey law for project-level matters** (for example, because the Sites are in New Jersey):
   - agree a single governing law and a single forum for *all* documents, so the parties at least avoid split law and parallel forums; and
   - negotiate a neutral forum (for example, the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey) rather than Treikev's home county court.
